articles.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
articles.text:
Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.

BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell secondhand Lego sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.

It was originally set up by a fan, but Lego acquired it in 2019. In a homepage message, the firm said that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.

"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site has been breached or hacked, and whether any customer data was affected.

After being contacted by the BBC, Lego published the update.

BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.

Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.

She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform, after she had already paid for it.

She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.

articles.title: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog
articles.text:
A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions.

The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use".

Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems.

The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly.

The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice.

"Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett.

"Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health."

Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers.

Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey.

Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
articles.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.

Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.

Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.

"They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said.

"It's not something that I did y'all," he continued. "It's something we did."

"In Mississippi, it's local people that make the difference."

Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.

The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.

"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.

"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.

"This is a historic election."

Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.

"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."

articles.title: Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in Labour and among other parties
articles.text:
There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.

Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."

It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.

And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.

Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off.

"There is a significant prize."

This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.

But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party.

Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.

The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.

Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain.

"We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."

But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship.

But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.

A voice from the past has a different set of concerns.

Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful".

The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal.

"If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem".

"How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."

For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.

The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.

Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.

Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.

articles.title: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins
articles.text:
Author M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.

Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.

The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.

Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."

Dame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."

Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.

While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world".

"He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said.

"Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."

The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.

The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.

He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."

He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."

That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said, external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said, external: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."

The Literary Review described it as, external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said, external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".

Another Telegraph critic wrote, external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books.

"And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday, Harrison explained how he had "wanted to write a book which really satirised the present-day barrage of information that we all suffer, without the necessary tools to understand what we're hearing and to analyse it and to have critical thinking about it".

He continued: "So the whole idea was to build a disaster in which it was a disaster of explanation, a disaster of the failure to understand the world as it was now."

articles.title: Ukraine's power supply close to critical as Russian strikes bring darkness and cold
articles.text:
Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.

"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."

This rolling schedule of planned power cuts has been in place since October, as Russia intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.

Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."

Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.

"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.

Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.

We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.

The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.

Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.

"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."

Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.

But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.

If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.

"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."

The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.

"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."

As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.

The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.

Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.

On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.

Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.

"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".

He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day.

"We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.

Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".

Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun.

"It's the worst feeling" Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"

When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.

The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness.

"I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."

Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko, Kamila Hrabchuk and Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title: New York building collapse kills at least two, officials say
articles.text:
At least two people have died and more than 17 others are injured after a building in New York City collapsed into an open construction site, officials have said.

It sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders at the scene in Brooklyn, trying to find survivors who may have been trapped under the rubble of the three-storey building.

Hours later, aerial video showed firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher.

Authorities are yet to determine what caused the sudden collapse at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday.

The rescue mission has been described as "extremely dangerous" by New York City Fire Department (FDNY) Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.

She added that people from the collapsed building and also the construction site had been trapped.

"Members have been working methodically and haven't stopped since they arrived this afternoon," Bonsignore said.

Some pictures of the collapsed building, on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, show an entire side of it gone, with bedrooms and closets exposed. Among the debris, smashed concrete and twisted metal, are household items and clothes.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined emergency responders at the scene, praising them for their rapid response.

They "arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers," he later wrote on X.

The Brooklyn building was built in 1930, city records show, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

articles.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.text:
Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Borthers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release funding in recent days.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £9m from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier. This will grant the company an additional 10 days to find a new buyer.

There are three bids currently on the table for Poundland, all of which have so far been rejected by the Gordon Brothers, who stand to profit from selling the company and its stock piecemeal.

Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".

"They refused to prioritise, protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he added.

"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."

Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".

He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".

"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business, and particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.

Following the private meeting with MPs, Poundland's chief executive Barry Williams told the BBC the chain's board would hold an urgent meeting on Wednesday night.

articles.title: Some Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
articles.text:
Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.

Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

articles.title: From Paris to DC - why offices are being turned into apartments
articles.text:
When Roland Cubin walks you round what will eventually be a new Parisian apartment you have to use your imagination.

"Here you will be in the kitchen, and here is the bathroom," says the deputy CEO of French real estate company Groupama Immobilier.

It all sounds appealing, an upmarket flat in the west of Paris, but presently the space doesn't look like one at all. That's because it's currently a corner of one floor of a nine-storey office building called Le Diamant, where 1,800 people work.

Groupama Immobilier intends to convert the entire building into apartments. It should be the first of many such office-to-apartments conversions in the surrounding area.

We are in La Défense, the purpose-built, business district of the French capital, where the city has congregated its modern skyscrapers.

Mirroring a similar trend in places such as New York, Washington DC and London; Paris La Défense, the public development authority that runs the area, has unveiled plans to turn up to a fifth of the office buildings into housing.

Cubin leads us into what is currently a conference room in the centre of the building. It has no windows, which is indicative of a big challenge when turning offices into apartments – what to do with the large amount of space in the middle of every floor that doesn't get any natural light.

"There won't be any rooms there. Just access," says Roland Cubin, in reference to lifts and stairs.

Other issues include the need for more plumbing, and ceilings that can be too low.

Despite these challenges, there is a simple reason why there are plans for so many conversions – demand for offices in La Défense and across Paris has plummeted since the Covid-19 pandemic and the growth of homeworking.

"La Défense has a vacancy rate of 14-15% which is higher than it used to be," says Pierre-Yves Guice, CEO of Paris La Défense.

He adds that another reason for the conversion programme is the need to transform the business district from a place where the only thing people do is work.

"To retain companies in France and in Western Europe we need to diversify these office landscapes of the last century, because no-one wants to work in such an environment any longer," says Guice.

Ludovic Delaisse, CEO of the French arm of the Canadian real estate business Colliers, says that demand for office space in Paris has fallen by almost a third over the past five to six years.

He adds that office high rises will continue to be needed, but that cities need to make sure that leisure time can be enjoyed around them, such as having restaurants, bars, cinemas and gyms on their doorstep.

"People like the idea of grouping together in a centre of expertise [for work] - in tech hubs, for example. The challenge for La Défense is to be a place where you want to be, that you want to see when you leave work in the evening."

Inspiration for La Défense can come from Washington DC and New York City, where tax cuts for property developers are fuelling the largest amount of office to apartment conversions in the US. Like in Paris, this is in response to falling demand for office space since the pandemic.

A report last year, external found that 8,310 converted flats were in the pipeline in New York, and 6,533 in Washington.

In third place was Los Angeles on 4,322, followed by Chicago on 3,606.

"We set a goal of introducing 15,000 new residents downtown by 2028 and we are now on track to doing that," says Washington DC's deputy mayor for planning and development Nina Albert.

She says that while "there may be one or two pretty significant building demolitions… the majority are office conversions".

As in Paris, they've faced technical challenges. They've sometimes solved the natural light problem in the middle of office buildings by creating atriums – light sinks in other words – in the middle of them.

Albert adds that about "hundreds of millions of dollars of private investment" has flooded into the sector.

In addition to tax cuts, the DC Department of Buildings, part of the Council of the District of Columbia, has eased planning restrictions to make it easier for office conversion schemes to gain official approval in the US capital. It's a similar case in New York City.

In the UK, there are also tax cuts and eased planning rules, external for converting offices into apartments. This has led to a continuing boom in conversions. A report last year by property firm Knight Frank said that the number of such projects in London were 60% higher , externalthan pre-Covid levels.

Back in Paris, Cubin hopes that French authorities follow these examples and reduce both taxes and rules regarding conversions.

"Just how the government deals with the tax question will decide whether France will be able to convert 2% of its vacant offices or 18 to 23%," he says.

"And at the moment, when you transform a building in a way that changes its function, it is classed not as an old building that's been changed but as a new building with all the regulatory demands that go with that regarding car parking spaces, wheelchair access, fire safety and so on."

articles.title: Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
articles.text:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.

It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.

The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.

There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.

In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.

However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".

She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."

Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.

articles.title: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.text:
Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.

Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
articles.text:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.

"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,

"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."

Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".

She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.

Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".

"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

articles.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
articles.text:
US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.

Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.

However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.

The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.

However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.

While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.

For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.

When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

articles.title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
articles.text:
Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.

She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.

But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action.

Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.

Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.

After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.

Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.

This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.

Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process.

"I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."

Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.

In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.

After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.

Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.

She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest.

In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.

But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December.

"It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says.

"I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."

Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."

The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.

Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

articles.title: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
articles.text:
Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

Early odds suggest a Democrat may win the presidential election in two years, a fitting coda to last week’s broad rejection of the Maga brand of politics. It’s not beyond hope to expect a Democratic trifecta that will spend less time on settling grievances and more on fixing a threadbare social safety net that allows for the deepest poverty in the affluent world.

And yet, the post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money. The federal deficit is now running at about 6.2% of GDP. The federal debt hit $40tn, more than 120% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Paying interest on that debt costs some 3.2% of GDP. That’s about $1tn, more than is spent on national defense. The Congressional Budget Office projects that debt and interest payments will continue to grow faster than the economy over the coming decades. In October alone, the first month of the 2027 fiscal year, the fiscal deficit ballooned to $409bn.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that restoring the subsidies to health insurance plans under Obamacare from 2030 to 2039 would cost $460bn. Undoing the budget cuts to the Snap food stamp program and Medicaid that Trump used to partly fund the tax cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would cost $2.2tn over that decade. “Reversing the harms is going to be very expensive,” said CBPP’s senior director for Federal budget policy, Brendan Duke.

And that’s the easy part. The trust fund that pays for social security benefits is scheduled to run out of money in less than six years, when the new crop of Democratic senators are still in their first term. By law, that would lead to an automatic 22% cut in benefits. Fixing that will require more money. Artificial intelligence may further complicate the picture, burdening the safety net with potentially millions of workers displaced by the new technological revolution.

Historian Bruce Bartlett, who back in the day advised Ronald Reagan on budget policy, argues that this state of affairs is the outcome of a Republican strategy honed over the years since Gipper’s day: cut taxes to strangle the budget and tie the hands of whatever Democratic administration comes next.

Trump’s OBBBA will add somewhere between $4.1tn and $5.5tn to the federal debt over 10 years, depending on whether temporary tax cuts in the bill are made permanent by a future Congress, something that has usually happened in the past. This, Bartlett once told me, will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”.

The new taxes that would be needed just to fill the holes Trump and his Republican enablers bored into the budget, let alone patch up the safety net they gleefully eviscerated, seem beyond anything achieved in recent memory.

Consider this: The last time that a government with any Republican in power delivered a tax increase was in the 1990s, when George HW Bush was president and Congress was blue. Bush paid for his sin, though, losing reelection to Democrat Bill Clinton. And that was the end of that.

Democrats have raised money when they held the presidency and Congress. But the trend suggests the opportunities are fading. Bill Clinton’s 1993 tax increases are estimated to yield the equivalent of $3.3tn over the 2030-2039 decade, adjusting for inflation. But the feat, which helped produce the nation’s first budget surplus since the 1960s, was ultimately spent on a tax cut by Clinton’s successor, George W. Bush.

The next shot at raising taxes was more modest. Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act raised the equivalent of $1.1tn over 2030-2039, in inflation-adjusted dollars. But Obama also made permanent some of George W Bush’s tax cuts. Joe Biden tried to go bigger: his original Build Back Better Act, passed in the House, would have raised the equivalent of $2.3tn over that window. But the Senate nixed that, authorizing only about $700bn in the Inflation Reduction Act.

How much more tax revenue does the US need? It depends on what Democrats want to achieve. Total tax revenue in the US amounts to less than 26% of its gross domestic product. That is 9 percentage points less than Britain’s total tax take, as a share of its economy, 9.5 points less than Canada’s, 12.5 points less than Germany’s and 16 percentage points less than Sweden’s.

Perhaps matching other rich countries is an impossibly high bar. Still, Democrats must prove that they understand the new America they hope to build comes with a price tag they are willing to fight for.

Some tax cuts in Trump’s OBBBA are set to expire in the next couple of years: exemptions on income from tips and overtime, a new deduction for seniors and an increase in the deduction for state and local taxes. The CBPP observed that these cuts offer next to nothing to Americans on the bottom rungs of the income distribution. Extending them would cost about $1.2tn over the 10-year window.

Will Democrats have the guts to end them? That will be the test of whether America is ready for a new social contract or not.

articles.title: Federal judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed
articles.text:
Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

The judge noted the significance of the documentary’s editing decision, which spliced together comments made by Trump that were nearly 55 minutes apart, something the BBC has apologized for.

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” he wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The judge continued: “Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

The judge noted past errors in the broadcaster’s coverage and wrote that “such examples can be said to be probative of BBC’s state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC’s non-action toward false statements about Trump. Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump.”

The judge also wrote that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

The BBC released a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Trump heralded the ruling on Truth Social, calling it a “huge victory”. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump said.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

And the judge determined that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

articles.title: US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped
articles.text:
US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

But the newest data shows that prices are still increasing at a moderate pace. Economists estimate that, if interpolating the data for October 2025, the topline inflation figure for October 2026 would have been 3.9%, according to Oxford Economics. That would have been the highest its been since May 2026, when inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high.

Higher energy costs driven by the Iran war have been the main factor behind increased inflation. Energy prices continued to rise slightly in October, rising 0.7% after going up 5.2% in September. In September, the overall monthly change in CPI from August was 0.6%.

The new data comes after a midterm election that will give Democrats control of Congress, in what was largely seen as a rebuke of Republicans over high prices. In their postmortem of the midterms, Republicans, including JD Vance, have specifically pointed to frustration over increased gas prices as a reason why the party fared so poorly in the election.

Gas prices cooled slightly in October, dropping from an average of $4.41 a gallon at the beginning of the month to $4.22 a gallon, prices are still more than $1 a gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA. On Monday, the average price for a gallon at the pump fell below $4 for the first time since July.

The cost of diesel, which is used to power trucks, farming equipment, buses and trains, is nearly $2.50 a gallon higher compared with prices last year but has also been going down since October. Gas prices have continued to drop.

In September, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and are expected to hike rates again at their next meeting in December. Higher interest rates slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive, and can slow inflation. The Fed’s target inflation rate is 2%, which it considers a stable pace for price increases.

Growth in the labor market surpassed economists’ expectations in October, giving more room for the Fed to hike rates. The unemployment rate has been relatively steady, hovering just above 4%.

Because today’s inflation is so closely tied to energy prices, it’s unclear how much and how quickly a rate hike could ease prices. But the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank is dedicated to making sure price increases ease up.

“Our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” Warsh said on 28 October.

Consumer sentiment increased slightly at the end of October as gas prices eased, according to the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers. At the same time, the US stock market was experiencing a dip as investors voiced skepticism over the influx of AI spending.

“While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of ​a relatively ​turbulent period ⁠in stock markets,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, in a statement. “Moreover, ​consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over ​a ⁠possible AI bubble.”

articles.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued in US over affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.text:
Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, have been accused of misleading shareholders in a lawsuit over the Chinese spying scandal engulfing the $4.3tn (£3.2tn) company.

The legal action came as Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

According to a complaint filed in federal court in ​California, Nvidia and Huang misled shareholders in connection with the executive’s alleged ​affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based ⁠Megaspeed, who is not related to him.

The lawsuit claims both parties did ​not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that threatened the chipmaker’s reputation and business prospects.

The New York Times reported on the alleged relationship last month, and said US authorities had concluded Alice Huang ​was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia described its executive’s interaction with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” in a comment submitted to the New York Times last month, adding that “meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year”.

On Sunday, Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, without identifying the person involved in the affair.

The lawsuit claims the NYT statement was “materially false and misleading at the time it was made because Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang.”

It also accused the company of making false and misleading statements about its relationship with Megaspeed, which has reportedly been investigated over suspicions that it may have been diverting Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export restrictions.

Huang said in an interview published on 30 October that “we’ve studied all their [Megaspeed] deployments of our GPUs and counted every one”. He added: “And I think the US government also has as well.”

In a statement last year Megaspeed said it has acted “fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations”.

Nvidia announced on Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Shares in the company fell on Monday, closing down 4.3%, reducing Nvidia’s ​market ⁠value by approximately $190bn. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed.

Nvidia and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to ​a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the California company as it became the world’s most valuable chipmaker and made him ​one of the ​world’s most ⁠prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom.

It is common for shareholders to ⁠sue ​companies after unexpected share price declines. ​Nvidia shareholders, led by Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor, are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants in the class action suit, the term for a legal action where a person or small group of people sues an entity on behalf of a larger group.

Several US law firms have announced investigations into whether Nvidia misled investors and have asked shareholders to get in touch.

Trump said on Monday that the FBI is investigating Huang’s affair but said he did not think the executive had a reason to worry.

“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right, how you’re doing,” Trump said. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Huang said in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website: “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,”

Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Man Utd manager: Mauricio Pochettino's decade-long courtship - but Michael Carrick deserves better
articles.text:
When the expected formalities of Michael Carrick's dismissal as Manchester United manager are completed after a summit meeting in Monaco, Mauricio Pochettino looks set to turn a decade-long courtship with Old Trafford into a full-blown relationship.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment at Scott's restaurant in Mayfair with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016.

Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham, where he fashioned an intense, all-out-attacking team that the great Scot admired.

Pochettino called it "a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice".

In that moment, a link was forged.

Pochettino was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Jose Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018.

Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Erik ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.

Finally, as Carrick awaits what looks to be the inevitable, it looks like Pochettino will inherit the Old Trafford empire.

The problem for Pochettino is that the once great footballing empire is crumbling before the eyes, the dysfunctional product of years of poor decision-making and questionable appointments, allied to a Frankenstein's monster of a squad assembled by six managers.

One of Pochettino's quirks is to have a box of lemons in his office, believing they absorb negative energy. He will need several truckloads of the industrial strength variety to suck away the current mood at Old Trafford.

First things first, however, and that means waiting for the official confirmation of Carrick's departure, a long drawn-out affair which does little credit to part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

Carrick, 45, has proved to be out of his depth since being confirmed as permanent head coach following a successful interim spell, but his history of success as a player, his basic decency and his obvious desire to turn United's fortunes around makes the ham-fisted handling of his sacking another uncomfortable episode.

It is an emotion reflected by United's increasingly disaffected fanbase, who have made it clear who they blame for their current place in the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino's appointment would land in the middle ground between the flawed sentimentalism of turning to fan favourites with little or no track record of success, such as Carrick and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, as well as the quick fix of bringing in proven past winners such as Van Gaal and Mourinho.

With his one-time dream of returning to Spurs now seemingly out of reach forever, Pochettino is ready to pick up the reins at the fallen giants that are United, another club he has clearly always had in his sights.

He is currently coach of the USA, whom he led at this summer's World Cup, but even then United were lurking on his agenda.

During the campaign Pochettino held court with invited journalists at the USA team hotel in California.

When mention was made of United, Pochettino turned to his closest confidante and ever-present assistant coach Jesus Perez to say: "One day, your dream comes true. You go to Manchester United."

Perez replied with "United should have got you", promoting the response from a smiling Pochettino: "Future. Future."

Now the future is here.

The big question now is what Pochettino will United be getting?

He remains a beloved figure at Spurs, where he had an outstanding record of consistency following his appointment from Southampton in May 2014.

He never finished lower than fifth - in his first season - in any full campaign in charge, including second place behind Chelsea in 2016-17 and third in 2015-16 and 2017-18.

The one question mark always placed against Pochettino, including when he finished sixth at Chelsea in 2023-24, was an inability to get his teams over the line to tangible success in England.

Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with Paris St-Germain after leaving Spurs - the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title - but the club's hierarchy felt that was the minimum he should achieve given the squad at his disposal, and he did not see out his contract.

In England with Spurs, he was runner-up in the League Cup in 2014-15 and reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2016-17 and 2017-18. In 2018-19 he reached the Champions League final and the League Cup semis.

In one season at Chelsea - a loveless relationship in which he could never shed his Spurs connections in the eyes of fans - he reached the FA Cup semi-finals and lost the League Cup final.

Pochettino's driven, competitive nature means that is an itch he will want to scratch when his United appointment is confirmed.

While Spurs have always appeared to be his first love, there is also no doubt United occupies a special place in his thoughts.

Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who worked with Pochettino on his book Brave New World, says: "There is a fit with the people at the club too.

"Omar Berrada is a fan. When Manchester City drew up a shortlist to replace Pep Guardiola, some City supporters, including Omar, argued for Pochettino to be on it.

"There are plenty of clues about his feelings for United in the book. He was at the stadium in 1999 when United won the Champions League.

"Sir Alex Ferguson is mentioned 28 times, more than any other name in the biography.

"Spurs tried to push back and cut those references. Pochettino and I talked it over and decided that none of it would be touched. That shows how much it mattered to him."

Pochettino is a renowned builder, as he proved at Spurs after succeeding the sacked Tim Sherwood, working with Harry Kane to develop the recently crowned Ballon d'Or winner, as well as bringing Son Heung-Min to the club for a bargain £22m from Bayer Leverkusen in 2015.

If Pochettino can repeat that - a tough job in United's circumstances - and reproduce the easy-on-the-eye, attacking football played with relentless energy, then he could finally be the perfect fit Ratcliffe has so far looked in vain to discover.

Pochettino is also his own man, so it will be intriguing to see how he works with Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox.

The road to Pochettino's sacking at Spurs effectively started following a friendly win against Real Madrid only weeks after their Champions League final defeat, when he made it clear he was not having enough influence at the club.

He enjoys warm relationships with his players, with a track record of improvement. It was no co-incidence that Cole Palmer enjoyed his best season working under Pochettino at Chelsea, scoring 25 goals in 45 appearances.

Pochettino, however, is also single-minded and ruthless, as he proved with an emphatic response to criticism for not phoning the players he left out of the USA World Cup squad.

He said: "When I was a player, when I didn't make the roster I didn't want my coach to call me. The players who didn't make the roster, they don't want to hear me say 'I apologise'. What are you going to say? Am I going to lie?"

He will need to call on every one of those qualities if and when he assumes control at United.

Back to that lunch date with Ferguson.

The final word on that day went to Pochettino as the pair argued over who was picking up the tab.

Ferguson said Pochettino could pay if he named an Argentina player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.

Pochettino, in what he claimed was a moment of inspiration, named Guillermo Stabile.

He won that argument. Now both he and Ferguson will hope Pochettino can produce more moments of inspiration to win something more substantial at United.

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.
articles.text:
Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.

United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.

Once Carrick's future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.

US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United - and sources have told BBC Sport they have a contingency plan for their manager leaving, which includes a succession plan.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.

The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.

The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week.

With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games.

On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager.

Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.

United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions - when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.

Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday that will be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.

On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.

It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.

Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday.

United are 18th in the Premier League - inside the relegation zone - after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.

It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.

Pochettino's first job in the Premier League was at Southampton from January 2013, before a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance.

He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea.

Pochettino moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024, and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.

While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football.

Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories - including from BBC Sport - came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace.

Going further back, Mark Hughes was replaced immediately by Roberto Mancini at Manchester City in 2009. Hughes' imminent dismissal was reported on the morning of his final game in charge.

It is impossible to reach that situation without talks taking place beforehand, and it would be naive to think they do not go on in a world in which agents are pushing clients for jobs that either do, or do not, exist or clubs are trying to gauge interest before making a decision.

I have been told by one source the Pochettino terms to join United are more or less agreed. I have also been told if they decide to push on, United can decide whether the former Spurs and Chelsea boss remains with the USA team for their matches against Haiti.

If he did stay, it would mean a sharp turnaround from a Tuesday night match - which finishes in the early hours of Wednesday - to be at Carrington for preparations before United's game against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

There are a lot of gaps to fill in yet, not least whether Carrick will be dismissed or not.

But it seems more likely there will be clarity on that on Wednesday, and from that the rest of the jigsaw pieces should start to slot into place.
